description: We’re a group of students interested in space, technology, AI, and science. We’re joining the NASA Space Apps Challenge and Space Mission Design Game to learn, gain experience, and build something exciting together.
summary:
We developed Project Selene, a browser-based 3D space mission game. Players design a spacecraft part by part in a Vehicle Assembly Bay, where every choice changes the budget, the mass and the power balance. Then they fly that same spacecraft themselves through hazards built from NASA open data: fireballs, meteorites, comets and near-Earth asteroids, scaled for gameplay.

It addresses the challenge by connecting design and operation in one loop. Students usually learn orbits, power and other space topics as separate chapters, but real missions fail where those pieces meet. In Project Selene, a weak design decision shows up later in flight, and players meet real NASA datasets through play instead of a spreadsheet.

This matters because failure becomes safe and useful. A student with only a browser can run a whole mission, take a hit, see their score, redesign and fly again. That loop is how engineers learn, and we plan to bring it to more classrooms with team mode and Bangla language support.
details:
What it does and how it works
Project Selene is a 3D space mission game that runs in a web browser. It has three stages:

  1. Briefing: Mission Control shows the mission of the day (a real near-Earth object, the same target for every player), the Hall of Fame and the NASA datasets behind the game.
  2. Design: in the Vehicle Assembly Bay, players pick a command core, engine, fuel tank, power system, science instrument and shield from a parts catalog. Each part has real trade-offs, and a live panel tracks budget, mass against the launcher limit, delta-v, thrust and net power. A flight clearance check lists what is missing or risky before launch.
  3. Flight: players fly the spacecraft they built, with pitch, yaw, roll and main burn, live telemetry and a near-Earth object radar. Meteor showers arrive with only seconds of warning, and players can shoot, dodge, use the shield or repair damage on a spacewalk. Every run is scored.

Benefits
Design and operation are connected, so a weak design choice shows up later in flight. Students meet real NASA data through play, and failure is safe: take a hit, see the score, redesign, fly again.

Intended impact
We want any student with a browser to be able to run a whole mission instead of learning each topic in isolation. Next steps are team mode for four players, a post-mission report that explains why a mission failed, and Bangla language support.

Tools and data

  • Software: JavaScript with ES modules, [3D library], [other tools, hosting].
  • NASA data: the NeoWs near-Earth object API (live), plus fireball, meteorite landing, near-Earth comet, WISE/NEOWISE and spacewalk (EVA) records.
  • How the data is used: fireballs set meteor size and speed, comets and WISE objects set targets and difficulty, meteorites drive sample payloads, and EVA records set crew time and repairs.

How it is creative
Instead of a simulator or a quiz, it turns systems engineering into a build-then-fly loop. The hazards are scaled from real records, and short “real data insight” facts appear during flight.

Factors we considered

  • Access: it runs in a browser with no install, so it works on school computers.
  • Accuracy versus fun: real values are scaled so the game stays playable.
  • Learning from failure: runs are short and scored, so retrying is quick
